extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, academic researchers, and others interested in peer review policy and reviewer motivation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical findings about policies to motivate reviewers and improve peer review timeliness and (where measurable) quality: deadlines, monetary and social incentives, reminders, recognition, templates, assignment/enforcement practices, and potential market/ethical effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness / Deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Shortened reviewer deadlines (e.g., 6 weeks → 4 weeks) reduce median review times; most reviewers submit their review just prior to the deadline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chetty reported shortening the deadline from 6 to 4 weeks reduced median review times by 12 days (48 → 36). ‘‘If you shorten the deadline by two weeks you receive reviews two weeks earlier on average.’’ Note: much of the speedup occurs in the last week before a deadline; setting shorter deadlines can shift when reviewers do their work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetary incentives (cash payments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing cash rewards for meeting a short deadline can further reduce review times (e.g., $100 for meeting a 4-week deadline reduced times an additional 8 days).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cash incentives increased submissions clustered just before deadline (rush effect). Chetty found no evidence that reviewers reverted to slower practices after incentives stopped. However, concerns exist about pricing (too low can offend), affordability for journals, potential crowding out of intrinsic motives, and potential impacts on decision-making or market dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social incentives (publicity/recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Telling reviewers their reviewing times would be posted publicly produced modest reductions in review times (~2.5 days) and had larger effects for tenured faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social incentives are weaker than cash or deadline changes but may influence certain subgroups. Combining reputational and monetary incentives can attract different participants for different reasons; there is no reason that both couldn't coexist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measured review quality (editor-followed decisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: One empirical measure of review quality used was whether editors followed the reviewers' recommendations (used by Chetty et al.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shorter deadlines slightly reduced report length but did not affect this quality proxy. Be cautious: 'editor-followed decisions' is an imperfect proxy for review substance; other measures may be needed to evaluate quality comprehensively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reminder timing and frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: When reminders are sent has a strong effect on when reviewers complete reviews; many reviewers act when reminded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changing reminder structure (e.g., from 5 days before to 10 and 15 days before) enabled journals to shorten overall deadlines (e.g., move from 45 to 30 days) without losing reviewers. Multiple, earlier reminders can prompt action earlier than a single late reminder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition programs (non-monetary rewards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal recognition (Outstanding Reviewer lists, certificates, letters to department chairs) can motivate reviewers and acknowledge contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition requires staff work but can pay dividends: posting names, sending certificates, and notifying supervisors were reported as effective practices to reward and motivate reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured reviewer guidance and templates
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing better reviewer guidelines and a fillable/template review form improves reviewer experience and consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journal Prep offered 7–10 day reviews with a flexible fillable PDF template developed because several reviewers asked for 'better reviewer guidelines.' Templates can standardize expectations across disciplines and make it easier for reviewers to deliver usable reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banking / credit models for reviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Credit or banking systems (e.g., reviewers earn credits that let them queue their own manuscripts) are an alternative to direct payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the B.E. Journal banking model and PubCred proposals; such systems create reciprocal incentives within a publisher/community rather than cash payments, and may shape reviewer supply differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed vs variable incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixed material incentives perform worse than other incentive types; variable incentives tied to outcomes may work better but are difficult to implement for journal peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lab experiments and field data suggest fixed payments (same payment for any on-time review) can be counterproductive, while outcome-dependent (variable) incentives could align incentives better but pose measurement and fairness challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowding out and ethical/corruption risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Monetary incentives can 'crowd out' intrinsic, prosocial motives and may introduce risks of dishonest or biased reviewing if compensation interacts with editorial incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners warn 'wherever money enters, honesty and objectivity gets out'; concerns include editors pressuring reviewers, changes to decision-making to preserve revenue, and corruption if pay becomes linked to favorable outcomes. Use caution and monitoring when introducing payments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affordability and market effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Paying reviewers could create a market where journals compete on reviewer compensation, advantaging wealthy publishers and possibly changing journal prestige dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commentators predict higher pay for scarce expertise and potential global inequities (e.g., reviewers from poorer regions reviewing for richer journals). Consider long-term sustainability and effects on smaller publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to review depends on manuscript quality and pay level
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are less willing to review unintelligible or poorly written manuscripts even for money; modest payments may not compensate for low-quality submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In an informal poll, respondents said $100 would not be worth reviewing an unintelligible paper. Therefore payment level must match the perceived effort and manuscript quality; otherwise, reviewers may decline or provide low-effort reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spillover effects across journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Changing incentives at one journal did not detectably affect reviewers' willingness to review or review times at other journals (in Chetty's study limited to 20 Elsevier economics journals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical evidence suggests localized incentive experiments may not immediately change broader reviewing behavior, but longer-term market shifts could differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement and transparency of review contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Two approaches to acknowledging review activity are 'open peer review' (publishing full reports) and 'summary information' (counts of reviews); each has trade-offs for transparency and reviewer protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open peer review could disadvantage reviewers recommending rejection unless all reports are published; summary counts are easier but don't assess review quality. Emerging solutions include DOIs for review reports and integration with identifiers like ORCID.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heterogeneity in reviewer quality and predictors
rubrics_metrics.description: Review quality is heterogeneous: some reports are worthless, others are highly insightful. Career stage, institutional prestige, or h-index do not reliably predict review quality; initial reviews are predictive of later performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should not assume seniority equates to review quality; early review performance can be used to identify consistent good reviewers. Consider tracking reviewer quality over time rather than relying on status proxies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign more reviewers / simultaneous assignment strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Assigning more reviewers than strictly needed and sending assignments simultaneously can reduce time spent on follow-up and increase the chance of timely completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medwave assigned all reviewers at once and used over-assignment; when two reviews didn't arrive, they reassigned a new batch. This approach facilitates timeliness but increases editorial workload and cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement policies for non-compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear enforcement (e.g., disinviting reviewers who miss deadlines, not granting extensions) can improve compliance with timeliness expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medwave reported disinviting late reviewers (no extra days allowed) and escalating reminders (what one commenter called 'harassment') before deadlines; strict enforcement can improve response rates but risks alienating reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Token incentives can backfire
rubrics_metrics.description: Small token payments (e.g., $10 book coupon, $25 honoraria) can frustrate reviewers and be perceived as insulting rather than motivating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Company of Biologists discontinued their $25 token payment because transaction costs and negative reactions outweighed benefits. Match reward type/size to reviewer expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition integration with career assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Formalizing peer review contributions in promotion and research assessment could incentivize higher-quality reviewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making review reports or validated counts discoverable to stakeholders (publishers, funders, institutions) and integrating them into evaluation (via ORCID/CASRAI specs, DOIs for reviews) may increase reviewer motivation and reward quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off between speed and quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies that speed up reviews (short deadlines, cash incentives) may slightly reduce report length but do not necessarily reduce measured quality; however, quality is a separate dimension requiring its own safeguards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should evaluate both timeliness and substantive quality separately; speeding up timelines should be accompanied by monitoring for perfunctory reviews, use of quality metrics, and reviewer selection/training to maintain standards.
